title: Japan’s mission to Martian moon and back underway
description: This mission is expected to be the first-ever Martian moon landing. At 4:41 a.m. on 20 October, an H3 rocket took off from the Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima Prefecture. It was carrying the MMX (Martian Moons eXploration), one of Japan’s largest-ever spacecraft, with a weight of 4,480 kilograms (9,877 pounds), and as of this […]
content:
This mission is expected to be the first-ever Martian moon landing.

At 4:41 a.m. on 20 October, an H3 rocket took off from the Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima Prefecture. It was carrying the MMX (Martian Moons eXploration), one of Japan’s largest-ever spacecraft, with a weight of 4,480 kilograms (9,877 pounds), and as of this writing, all systems are operating normally.

▼ And was there ever any doubt that there’s also a cute mascot version of MMX?

The MMX’s mission is to travel to Phobos, one of Mars’ moons, land there, pick up samples, and bring them back to Earth. It’s one of the most ambitious Mars missions to date, but Japan’s space agency JAXA has already made a name for itself by landing on asteroids and returning samples successfully on two previous endeavors.

Considering Phobos is up to ten times the size of those asteroids and locked into Mars’ orbit, this might seem like an easier mission. However, the key factor is overcoming the gravity of both Phobos and Mars. The MMX will have to make a soft landing on Phobos, then take off again in order to return to Earth. As a result, about 68 percent of the spacecraft’s total weight is just propellant.

It is hoped that by collecting material on Phobos, we can learn more about how it and Mars’ other moon, Deimos, were formed. The two leading theories are that they were once asteroids that got captured by Mars’ gravity or that they formed from the debris expelled by a massive collision of something with the red planet. In addition, it is said that about 0.1 percent of material on Phobos is actually Martian soil, having been ejected when meteorites struck the planet. The goal of the MMX is to pick up at least 10 grams of material from Phobos for an estimated 0.01 grams of actual Martian material.

▼ Here’s a simulation of how it should all go down in a nutshell.

Whether this will be the first sample from Mars transported by humans back to Earth remains to be seen, however. China is currently preparing to send its Tianwen-3 to Mars, where it will collect 500 grams of pure Martian soil and bring it back to Earth. Both projects are scheduled to return here in 2031, so if everything goes as planned for everyone, it’ll be a relative photo-finish to see which country will be the first to break off a piece of Mars and carry it back.

Going according to plan is a big “if” as well. The MMX was originally expected to launch in 2024, but development of the H3 was delayed and the very tight window when Earth and Mars are properly aligned once every two years closed. China will also need to make sure everything progresses like clockwork from now until their launch in 2028 to avoid their own two-year delay.

Regardless of whoever does get back first, these samples will help to blow open our understanding of the Martian environment, including the possibility that life once or even still exists there in some form. Then, maybe we can finally get back to checking out our neglected other neighbor Venus someday.

It’d be pretty funny if all this time there actually were a bunch of aliens living in those boiling sulphuric clouds, wondering why no one ever comes looking for them.

Source: Seizo Trend, JAXA, Tokyo Shimbun

title: Ghibli composer Joe Hisaishi named Composer-in-Residence of Los Angeles Philharmonic
description: Multiyear relationship will include new works specially created for L.A. audiences. At the age of 75 and with a career that’s already spanned more than 50 years, it wouldn’t be unnatural for Joe Hisaishi to be easing into retirement. Or maybe it would be, since the acclaimed composer best known for creating the soundtracks to […]
content:
Multiyear relationship will include new works specially created for L.A. audiences.

At the age of 75 and with a career that’s already spanned more than 50 years, it wouldn’t be unnatural for Joe Hisaishi to be easing into retirement. Or maybe it would be, since the acclaimed composer best known for creating the soundtracks to Studio Ghibli’s most beloved anime films, including My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, and Spirited Away, since Hisaishi continues to display a boundless passion and enthusiasm for making music and sharing it with as wide an audience as possible.

For example, en route to setting a couple of Guinness World Records, he held a series of concerts at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles over three days this past July. If you missed your chance to see him then, don’t worry, because Hisaishi has now been named Composer-in-Residence of the Los Angeles Philharmonic orchestra.

This isn’t some simple honorary title/goodwill ambassador deal either. The L.A. Phil is describing the relationship as “a five-year creative partnership” that will start with the upcoming 2027/2028 concert season. In addition to recurring performances at all three of the organization’s customary venues (the iconic hillside Hollywood Bowl, the adjacent John Anson Ford Amphitheatre, and the downtown Walt Disney Concert Hall), Hisaishi “will create new works specifically for the LA Phil and its audiences” while also engaging in new commissions, recording projects, and educational and community outreach endeavors.

“Los Angeles holds a special place in my musical life-from the premiere of my Harp Concerto with the LA Phil’s Emmanuel Ceysson at Walt Disney Concert Hall to our recent performances at the Hollywood Bowl and The Ford,” said Hisaishi following the announcement, and also that he’s “deeply honored” to be chosen for the role. “In the seasons ahead, I look forward to exploring new musical horizons with this extraordinary orchestra and sharing the spirit of discovery with audiences in Los Angeles and beyond.”

▼ An audio clip of one of Hisaishi’s previous Hollywood Bowl concerts

View this post on Instagram

▼ With Hisaishi scheduled to be spending a lot more time in L.A., he’ll also be able to check out America’s first One Piece store, should the mood strike him.

Hisaishi’s resume isn’t composed entirely of Ghibli soundtracks, as he’s also made contributed selected compositions or arrangements to other anime including Mobile Suit Gundam, Children of the Sea, Kimagure Orange Road, and Creamy Mami, as well as creating the soundtrack for video game Ni no Kuni and a handful of live-action Beat Takeshi movies. There’s no denying, though, that Hisaishi is most strongly associated with the work he’s done for Ghibli, As a matter of fact, there’s never been a Hayao Miyazaki-directed Ghibli feature film that Hisaishi didn’t write the score for, and with the studio’s track record of leaving a deep impression on fans around the world with its soundscapes, no doubt the new creative journey Hisaishi is about to embark on will be another movingly memorable one.

Source: Los Angeles Philharmonic via Anime News Network/Rafael Antonio Pineda

title: Japanese scientists developing cute, autonomously swarming robo dogs for anti-bear patrols [Video]
description: Hacchan is a mecha version of an Akita Inu hunting dog. Along with a bit of chilly autumn crispiness, there’s also some apprehension in the air in Japan. That’s because we’re getting to the part of the year when bears start bulking up in preparation of hibernating, which means they’ll be growing bolder and roaming […]
content:
Hacchan is a mecha version of an Akita Inu hunting dog.

Along with a bit of chilly autumn crispiness, there’s also some apprehension in the air in Japan. That’s because we’re getting to the part of the year when bears start bulking up in preparation of hibernating, which means they’ll be growing bolder and roaming wider in their search for stuff to eat,

With bear attacks having become a topic of heightened concern in recent years, and northern Japan having the country’s largest bear populations, earlier this year Akita Prefectural University began accepting proposals from faculty and students for its Bear-Tech Solution Contest. A total of 41 entries were submitted, and on October 13 a selection of the most promising ideas were presented in Akita City, including an idea for a surprisingly cute anti-bear robot dog.

Called Hacchan, the robot named after Japan’s most famous Akita Inu, Hachiko. Rather than hang out around Shibuya Station waiting for its master to come home and munching on grilled chicken handouts, though, Hacchan’s behavior is inspired by the Akita Inu hunting dogs that would accompany Akita Prefecture’s traditional huntsmen into the woods in days of yore.

▼ Hacchan can be seen at the point in the video queued here.

However, unlike actual hunting dogs, Hacchan has been created with a nonviolent outcome in mind. The quadrupedal robot is meant for deployment on the edge of farms or towns, and when its camera detects a bear, it uses an internal speaker to play the sound of a dog barking loudly in order to scare the animal off and make it retreat back into the woods. By sharing its location data, Hacchan can even call other units to the scene, creating a pack of robo dogs for a more intimidating presence, while also building a database of bear sighting and behavior to help the robots efficiently and autonomously patrol the outer edges of the community.

Researcher Masayuki Yoshida of the university’s Regional Collaboration and Research Promotion Center, who’s leading the development of Hacchan, says they hope to begin field testing the robot dogs before the end of the year.

Source: FNN Prime Online/Akita TV via Yahoo! Japan News, Akita Prefectural University, Yomiuri Shimbun
